title: Zaidi’s Militia Dilemma
gist: Crisis Group's Lahib Higel argues that drones launched from Iraq hitting Saudi Eastern Province oil facilities on July 27, 2026 and the U.S.-Saudi retaliatory strikes two days later expose new Iraqi PM Ali al-Zaidi's core dilemma: Iran-aligned militias embedded in the state can drag Baghdad into the U.S.-Iran war. She argues the Sept. 30 end of the anti-Islamic State coalition mission and the withdrawal of some 2,500 troops creates a bilateral opening, but that only incremental factional integration — not disarmament — is achievable without fracturing the Iraqi state.

themes.theme: Iraqi militias as a Gulf oil-supply risk vector

insights.claim: On July 27, 2026 drones reportedly launched from Iraq targeted oil facilities in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province, and two days later Saudi Arabia and the United States carried out coordinated strikes against Iran-backed factions, reportedly killing at least 20 militia members.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: Iraqi territory is now a launch platform for strikes on Saudi crude infrastructure, adding a second attack vector alongside the Houthis that a Hormuz-only settlement would not neutralize.
insights.locator: Upon taking office in May

insights.claim: Iraq's self-described resistance factions targeted not only U.S. assets inside Iraq but also U.S. bases and civilian infrastructure in Jordan, Syria and the Gulf during the recent U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: The threat radius from Iraqi militias spans four theaters, so regional infrastructure and energy risk premia should not be scoped to Iraq alone.
insights.locator: The recent U.S.-Israeli war with Iran underscored

insights.claim: So long as conflict between Washington and Tehran continues, Iraq's resistance factions are unlikely to surrender either their military capabilities or what they regard as their legitimate right to fight the United States.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: Militia attack risk is a function of the U.S.-Iran conflict state, not of Iraqi domestic reform — track the bilateral war, not Baghdad's disarmament rhetoric.
insights.locator: So long as conflict between Washington and Tehran continues

insights.claim: U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed that the coalition against the Islamic State will conclude its mission on Sept. 30, resulting in the withdrawal of some 2,500 troops currently stationed in Iraq.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: A hard date for the multilateral drawdown sets up a Q4 2026 inflection in Iraqi security arrangements and in the militias' stated casus belli.
insights.locator: During Zaidi’s visit to Washington

insights.claim: The multilateral security relationship that has defined U.S.-Iraqi ties for more than a decade is giving way to a bilateral one, letting Baghdad negotiate the scope and terms of security cooperation directly and be more clearly accountable for the arrangement at home.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: Bilateral framing gives Baghdad more agency and could support a more stable defense-cooperation and training pipeline than the expiring coalition structure.
insights.locator: Over time, however, Zaidi has an opportunity

insights.claim: The claim by Zaidi and his predecessor Mohammed Shia al-Sudani that the coalition's exit will improve state leverage over Iran-backed groups should not be overstated, because U.S. advisors will remain and the strongest factions are tied ideologically and operationally to Iran's Axis of Resistance rather than merely reacting to foreign troops.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: Do not treat the troop withdrawal as a de-risking event for Iraqi political violence — the militias' motivation is transnational and survives the drawdown.
insights.quote: The end of the coalition will therefore not end Iraq’s militia problem.
insights.locator: There is some logic to that claim

insights.claim: Baghdad's approach to the militias is not a conventional disarmament, demobilization and reintegration process but incremental integration negotiated faction by faction, because the groups are not a defeated insurgency and no comprehensive dismantlement plan exists.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: Expect slow, partial, deal-by-deal progress headlines rather than a single disarmament milestone — calibrate Iraq stability expectations accordingly.
insights.quote: What Baghdad is attempting instead is incremental integration through negotiations with individual factions.
insights.locator: The government’s emerging approach

insights.claim: Muqtada al-Sadr's Saraya al-Salam was the first faction to hand control of its PMF brigades to Zaidi as commander in chief in June, with Qais al-Khazali's Asaib Ahl al-Haq and Shibl al-Zaidi's Kataib al-Imam Ali pledging to follow on unclear timetables.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: Faction-by-faction handovers are the concrete metric of Iraqi state consolidation to track, and Sadr's move is the template.
insights.locator: Muqtada al-Sadr’s Saraya al-Salam was the first

insights.claim: The factions most closely identified with the resistance — Kataib Hezbollah, Harakat al-Nujaba, Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada and Harakat Ansar Allah al-Awfiya — have publicly rejected integration even as some appear to be in discussions with the government.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: These four named groups are the residual attack risk that no Iraqi political process is currently on track to contain.
insights.locator: The factions most closely identified with the resistance

insights.claim: The strongest resistance factions retain missiles, drones and other advanced Iranian-supplied weapons stored in facilities beyond government access, including bases such as Jurf al-Sakhar, and bringing those arsenals under state authority would require a direct confrontation successive governments have avoided.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: Militia strike capability against Gulf energy targets is physically intact and out of Baghdad's reach regardless of personnel-integration progress.
insights.locator: The government is far less likely

insights.claim: Attempting to seize the militias' arsenals while the United States and Iran remain locked in open hostilities could strengthen the factions, weaken the government and ultimately fracture the Iraqi state.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: U.S. pressure for rapid disarmament is the scenario most likely to trigger Iraqi state fragmentation — a tail risk for Iraqi oil output and Kurdistan-federal relations.
insights.locator: Attempting it while the United States and Iran

insights.claim: The realistic near-term objective is that units receiving state salaries and formally belonging to the security apparatus answer to the commander in chief rather than to factional leaders, with the Joint Operations Command inventorying formal capabilities and establishing clearer chains of command.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: Payroll and chain-of-command control, not weapons seizure, is the measurable benchmark for Iraqi state capacity — a lower bar that is actually achievable.
insights.quote: Total disarmament ought not be the sole measure of progress.
insights.locator: Total disarmament ought not be the sole measure

themes.theme: Escalation management and the March-April precedent

insights.claim: During the March and April round of fighting, fear of domestic backlash made Baghdad reluctant to name the groups that attacked U.S. targets, so when U.S. retaliatory strikes killed Iraqi regular armed forces personnel who had not participated, the government appeared to accept U.S. military action against its own security institutions.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: Ambiguous attribution converts every U.S. retaliation into an Iraqi domestic legitimacy crisis, a mechanism that raises the odds of a rupture in U.S.-Iraq ties.
insights.locator: During the previous round of fighting in March and April

insights.claim: Clearer command structures would let the Iraqi government isolate attack perpetrators, protect uninvolved units and respond without treating the entire Popular Mobilization Forces as a single hostile bloc.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: Command-structure clarity is the practical de-escalation lever to watch, more predictive of contained escalation than diplomatic statements.
insights.locator: Clearer command structures would give the government

insights.claim: Zaidi's response to the Saudi-U.S. retaliatory strikes was more measured than his predecessor's — he canceled a planned Riyadh visit but refrained from summoning the Saudi ambassador, implicitly acknowledging Riyadh's self-defense claim.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: Baghdad's restraint signals it is trying to keep the Saudi relationship alive, lowering the odds of an Iraq-Gulf diplomatic rupture that would foreclose Gulf investment.
insights.locator: Yet Zaidi’s response to the recent Saudi-U.S. retaliatory strikes

insights.claim: Iraq's vulnerability to Iranian influence is reinforced by regional isolation and economic codependence, so expanding Gulf investment, energy links, trade and infrastructure is a more effective lever than pressure to disarm militias.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: Gulf capital flows into Iraq are the structural counterweight to Iranian leverage — track GCC-Iraq investment announcements as the real de-Iranization metric.
insights.quote: Greater Gulf investment and regional connectivity would give Baghdad stronger foundations for maintaining stability, restraining armed groups, and reducing the economic channels through which Tehran exercises influence.
insights.locator: The better objective is to expand Iraq’s strategic autonomy

insights.claim: Washington has already encouraged greater Iraq-Syria connectivity, including efforts surrounding the reconstruction of the Kirkuk-Baniyas oil pipeline, and should direct similar diplomatic energy toward Iraq's Gulf relations.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: A revived Kirkuk-Baniyas line would give Iraqi crude a Mediterranean outlet that bypasses Hormuz entirely — a concrete infrastructure trade tied to Syrian rehabilitation.
insights.locator: It has already encouraged greater connectivity

insights.claim: Turning Iraq into an anti-Iranian state is neither realistic nor desirable because Iran will remain a neighbor, a major trading partner and an influential political actor; the achievable goal is avoiding overwhelming dependence on any single external partner.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: Policy scenarios premised on flipping Iraq out of Iran's orbit are mispriced; the realistic path is diversification, which is slower and less headline-generating.
insights.quote: The aim should not be to turn Iraq into an anti-Iranian state.
insights.locator: The aim should not be to turn Iraq

insights.claim: Some Gulf capitals now view Iraq as irretrievably embedded in an Iranian sphere of influence while others believe Iraq is too large and strategically important to abandon, a split that determines whether Gulf capital returns.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: Which Gulf view prevails is the swing variable for Iraqi reconstruction and energy financing over the next several years.
insights.locator: While some Gulf capitals increasingly view Iraq

themes.theme: Zaidi's political capital and its limits

insights.claim: Zaidi is a young businessman with no established political track record, unlike the veteran politicians who have dominated Iraq's post-2003 order, and that outsider profile appears to be one reason the Trump administration preferred him for the premiership.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: Washington has personally invested in Zaidi, which raises both the U.S. appetite to support Iraq commercially and the reputational cost if he fails.
insights.quote: Yet changing the occupant of the prime minister’s office does not change the system over which he presides.
insights.locator: Zaidi has presented himself as a break with the past

insights.claim: Zaidi signed some 50 memoranda of understanding on his first Washington state visit, but the author argues his premiership should not be judged by the number of agreements signed.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: Discount the MOU headline count when assessing actual U.S.-Iraq commercial follow-through; execution is constrained by Baghdad's fragmented political economy.
insights.quote: But the success of his premiership should not be measured by the number of agreements signed
insights.locator: He spent a week in Washington

insights.claim: Iraq's underlying constraints — an oil-dependent economy, a fragmented political system, powerful armed factions and the Washington-Tehran rivalry — may take decades to transform and cannot be commanded away by any prime minister.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: Iraq remains a structurally high-beta oil economy with weak institutional buffers; leadership changes do not warrant re-rating sovereign or project risk.
insights.locator: Zaidi cannot escape Iraq’s geography

insights.claim: Moving too slowly against the militias risks entrenching parallel chains of command while moving too aggressively risks provoking an intra-Shiite conflict the Iraqi state may be unable to contain.
insights.speaker: Lahib Higel
insights.so_what: The narrow corridor between paralysis and civil conflict defines Iraq's political risk band — both tails are bad for output continuity.
insights.quote: Moving too slowly risks entrenching parallel chains of command. Moving too aggressively risks provoking an intra-Shiite conflict that the Iraqi state may be unable to contain.
insights.locator: Zaidi will inherit the same dilemma
